grammar.title: Unless, Provided, As Long As
grammar.explanation:
Besides **if**, English has other words for conditions. **Unless** means *if … not*. I won't go **unless** you come too.

**Provided (that)** and **as long as** mean *only if*. You can borrow my car **as long as** you drive carefully.

Use **unless** with a positive verb, not a negative one. Say **unless** you come. Never say **unless** you don't come.

After **unless**, **provided**, and **as long as**, use the present simple. We say **unless** it rains, not **unless** it will rain.

**In case** is for precautions — things you do now because something might happen later. Take a coat **in case** it gets cold.

These words fit travel plans well. **Unless** we book the apartment early, there will be no rooms left. We'll stop at a B&B **as long as** we arrive before dark.
examples: *You can borrow my car **as long as** you drive carefully.*
*I'll go to the party **unless** you come.*
*Take a coat **in case** it gets cold later.*
*You can come **as long as** you're quiet.*
*I'll lend it to you **on condition that** you return it.*

practice.q: Rewrite with unless: If you don't book the apartment early, you won't get a room.
practice.a: Unless you book the apartment early, you won't get a room.

practice.q: Rewrite with as long as: You can stay at the B&B, but only if you arrive before dark.
practice.a: You can stay at the B&B as long as you arrive before dark.

practice.q: Rewrite with in case: Take medicine for airsickness, because you might feel airsick.
practice.a: Take medicine for airsickness in case you feel airsick.

practice.q: Rewrite with provided: We'll drive to the coast, but only if the weather is good.
practice.a: We'll drive to the coast provided the weather is good.
